items.titel: US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
items.anriss: Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.

absaetze.t: In Washington, DC, a group of lawmakers has ramped up calls to increase the United States federal minimum wage and eliminate the subminimum wage, otherwise known as the tipped wage.
The group of 17 lawmakers, which includes current and newly elected House members, is calling for passage of the Living Wage For All Act, which has been languishing since it was introduced in April.
The legislation’s original lead sponsors include Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois, Representative Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, also of Illinois, and Representative Analilia Mejia of New Jersey.
The bill aims to gradually raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, with different timelines depending on the size of the employer.

Brad Lander, a congressman-elect from Brooklyn, New York, who says he will join the bill as a co-sponsor when the next congressional session begins in January, told Al Jazeera: “Doing it federally is the right way to go. Tying it into broader legislation that raises the minimum wage for all workers is a great approach.”
For larger employers — those with more than 500 employees nationwide or at least $1bn in annual revenue — the increase would be completed by 2031. Smaller employers would have until 2038.
After that, the minimum wage would be maintained at two-thirds of the US median hourly wage, with annual adjustments to preserve that ratio.

The bill would also eliminate the separate subminimum wage for tipped workers, currently $2.13 an hour. Under the existing framework, employers can count workers’ tips towards their minimum-wage requirements.

While several states have raised their own minimum wages, the federal rate remains $7.25 an hour, where it has stood since 2009. Washington, DC, has the highest minimum wage of any US jurisdiction, at $18.40 an hour, followed by Washington state at $17.13. However, 20 states do not have a minimum wage higher than the federal rate. Those states include Texas, Georgia and Iowa.
Laws governing the subminimum wage also vary across states. Seven states require employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage before tips, including Alaska, California and Nevada.

Others, including New York, have higher tipped cash wages than the federal rate but allow employers to take a tip credit, meaning they can pay workers less than the standard minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference.
In New York, minimum wages vary by region. The rate is $17 an hour in New York City and its surrounding suburbs, and $16 an hour in the rest of the state.

For tipped workers outside the food service industry, the minimum cash wage is $14.15 in the New York City metropolitan area and $13.30 elsewhere in the state. For restaurant workers, those rates are $11.35 and $10.70, respectively.
The distinction is a point of contention for Lander.
“All workers deserve a raise. The 45 million working people who make less than $20 an hour deserve a raise, and the tipped subminimum wage is inexcusable at this point,” he said.
A long-term fight

The subminimum wage has long been viewed as a legacy of racial and economic inequalities that disproportionately affected Black Americans. When Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act in 1938, establishing the first federal minimum wage, it excluded categories of workers in domestic and agricultural occupations, which disproportionately employed Black Americans.

Congress extended federal minimum-wage protections to restaurant and other service workers in 1966. But rather than requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage, lawmakers established a separate tipped minimum wage, initially set at 50 percent of the standard federal rate. Employers could count customers’ tips towards the rest of a worker’s minimum-wage obligation. In 1996, Congress froze the federal tipped cash wage at $2.13 an hour, where it remains today.

The purchasing power of the standard federal minimum wage has also changed drastically. Adjusted for inflation, the $7.25 minimum wage in 2009 would be worth $11.32 today, meaning it has lost 36 percent of its purchasing power.

The federal minimum wage’s purchasing power peaked in 1968, when the rate was $1.60 an hour. Adjusted for inflation, that peak would be worth significantly more than the current minimum wage, representing a loss of roughly 53 percent in purchasing power.

The push to raise wages also has public support. A new poll released on Wednesday by One Fair Wage, an organisation that has long campaigned to eliminate the subminimum wage, found that 78 percent of voters considered raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour an important factor in their vote in the recent US midterm elections, where Republicans were dealt massive losses with the cost of living a key issue for voters.

“Washington has allowed the federal minimum wage to become increasingly disconnected from the economic reality facing American families,” Saru Jayaraman, president of One Fair Wage, said in a statement.
The push for the Living Wage For All Act comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in the new Congress.

The last major attempt to raise the federal minimum wage came during former President Joe Biden’s first year in office. Democrats sought to increase the rate from $7.25 to $15 an hour through the Raise the Wage Act of 2021, which was included in the original proposal for Biden’s American Rescue Plan.

Ultimately, the effort failed after the Senate rejected a motion to waive budgetary rules that would have allowed the minimum-wage increase to proceed. The March 2021 vote was 42–58, with all Republicans opposed, joined by seven Democrats and independent Senator Angus King of Maine, who caucuses with Democrats.
Although the legislation failed, Biden raised the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $15 an hour in 2022 through an executive order. President Donald Trump revoked that order in 2025.

items.titel: Espagne: le chanteur Julio Iglesias visé par une enquête pour agressions sexuelles
items.anriss: L'Audience nationale, la plus haute instance judiciaire espagnole, a annoncé, mercredi 18 novembre, l'ouverture d'une enquête pénale visant le chanteur Julio Iglesias, après des plaintes déposées par deux anciennes employées de ses …

absaetze.t: L'Audience nationale, la plus haute instance judiciaire espagnole, a annoncé, mercredi 18 novembre, l'ouverture d'une enquête pénale visant le chanteur Julio Iglesias, après des plaintes déposées par deux anciennes employées de ses résidences aux Caraïbes. Les deux femmes dénoncent des agressions sexuelles et des traitements humiliants et dégradants. L'artiste de 83 ans rejette catégoriquement ces accusations.
2 min Temps de lecture

Le parquet espagnol a revu sa position en octobre 2026, après le dépôt d'une seconde plainte en septembre. Une première procédure, engagée en janvier, avait été classée, la justice espagnole s'étant alors estimée incompétente pour juger des faits qui se seraient déroulés aux Bahamas et en République dominicaine.

Le juge Antonio Piña a déclaré recevable la plainte visant Julio Iglesias pour des délits contre la liberté sexuelle, des violences et des traitements dégradants. Il a toutefois rejeté les qualifications de traite d'êtres humains et d'atteinte au droit du travail également mentionnées dans la plainte.

Selon l'Audience nationale, cette décision repose sur les indices fournis, notamment le témoignage d'une plaignante, qui « constitue un début de preuve des faits justifiant l'ouverture de l'enquête pénale ».
Deux anciennes employées à l'origine des accusations

À l'origine de cette affaire : les témoignages de deux femmes, une employée de maison et une kinésithérapeute, embauchées entre janvier et octobre 2021 dans les luxueuses résidences de Julio Iglesias en République dominicaine et aux Bahamas. Elles affirment y avoir subi des agressions sexuelles et des traitements humiliants. Leurs témoignages ont été le point de départ d'une vaste enquête menée par le journal espagnol elDiario et la chaîne américaine Univision. Les deux médias ont notamment révélé un système de recrutement de jeunes femmes issues de quartiers pauvres.

Parmi les éléments examinés par la justice figure une photographie présentée par l'une des plaignantes. Selon le tribunal, elle montre un hématome sur un bras, compatible avec une saisie violente, ainsi que « deux marques » sur une cuisse pouvant correspondre à une morsure. La plaignante affirme que ces blessures sont liées à des « actes de nature sexuelle » auxquels elle aurait été contrainte. Les deux femmes ont été convoquées pour témoigner « en personne » devant le juge le 3 février 2027.

De son côté, Julio Iglesias nie l'ensemble des faits et menace de poursuivre les médias à l'origine des révélations. En janvier, le célèbre chanteur espagnol avait dénoncé des accusations « absolument fausses », assurant n'avoir jamais « agressé, contraint ou manqué de respect à quelque femme que ce soit ». Sollicités par l'AFP, ses avocats ont indiqué ne pas vouloir « faire de commentaires ».

items.titel: Israels Armee startet Einsatz in von Hamas kontrolliertem Gebiet
items.anriss: Trotz der Waffenruhe hat Israels Armee nach eigenen Angaben einen neuen Einsatz im Zentrum des Gazastreifens begonnen. Ziel des Angriffs sei Infrastruktur der Terrororganisation Hamas. Die Islamisten werfen Israel Eskalation vor.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Gazastreifen Israel startet Bodeneinsatz in Hamas-Gebiet

Trotz der Waffenruhe hat Israels Armee nach eigenen Angaben einen neuen Einsatz im Zentrum des Gazastreifens begonnen. Ziel des Angriffs sei Infrastruktur der Terrororganisation Hamas. Die Islamisten werfen Israel Eskalation vor.

Die israelische Armee hat im Zentrum des Gazastreifens nach eigenen Angaben eine Militäroperation begonnen. Augenzeugen zufolge drangen die Panzer westlich der Gelben Linie vor. Diese markiert das von Israel kontrollierte Gebiet, das rund zwei Drittel des Küstenstreifens umfasst.

Der Einsatz richte sich "gegen einen Terrortunnel", der eine direkte und unmittelbare Bedrohung für die israelischen Soldatinnen und Soldaten darstelle, wie die Armee auf X schrieb. Es handele sich um den ersten Bodeneinsatz in dem Gebiet seit der im Jahr 2025 vereinbarten Waffenruhe, sagten Anwohner.
Hamas wirft Israel Eskalation vor

Die für zivile Angelegenheiten in den Palästinensergebieten zuständige israelische Behörde Cogat rief die betroffenen Bewohnerinnen und Bewohner auf, das Gebiet für die Dauer des Einsatzes zu verlassen.

Die Terrororganisation Hamas warf Israel eine gefährliche Eskalation und eine eklatante Verletzung der Waffenruhe vor. Das israelische Militär erklärte dagegen, die Hamas habe sich zuletzt neu formiert und aufgerüstet. Die Armee bliebe "gemäß dem Waffenstillstandsabkommen im Einsatz", heißt es in dem Statement auf X.
Weitere Angriffe trotz Waffenruhe

Die Waffenruhe war im Oktober 2025 unter Vermittlung von US-Präsident Donald Trump ausgehandelt worden. Sie hatte die schweren Kämpfe im Gaza-Krieg beendet, Angriffe jedoch nicht vollständig unterbunden. Seit Beginn der Waffenruhe vor 13 Monaten sind nach Angaben der von der Hamas kontrollierten Gesundheitsbehörden im Gazastreifen mindestens 1.600 Palästinenser getötet worden. Auf israelischer Seite fielen dem Militär zufolge fünf Soldaten.

Der Krieg hatte im Oktober 2023 mit dem blutigen Terrorangriff der Hamas auf Israel begonnen, bei dem rund 1.200 Menschen - viele von ihnen Zivilisten - getötet wurden. Bei der darauffolgenden israelischen Offensive starben nach palästinensischen Angaben mehr als 74.000 Menschen im Gazastreifen.

items.titel: US Defence Secretary Hegseth reveals military partnership on Venezuela trip
items.anriss: Pete Hegseth says the agreement will include joint training and intelligence sharing with the Venezuelan military.

absaetze.t: Pete Hegseth says the agreement will include joint training and intelligence sharing with the Venezuelan military.
United States Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth has announced a new agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.

The Pentagon chief made a surprise visit to the Venezuelan capital of Caracas on Wednesday, becoming the latest in a series of high-level officials under US President Donald Trump to travel to the South American country.
During his stop, Hegseth revealed that the deal would include intelligence sharing and joint training for the two countries’ militaries.
“We see this as a reestablishment of our defence partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries,” he said.
Their shared aim would be “to stabilise Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all”, Hegseth added.
Hegseth was hosted by interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who has led the government since her swearing-in on January 5. His trip was not previously announced by the Pentagon.
The Trump administration has exerted heavy influence over Rodriguez and her government after abducting former President Nicolas Maduro during a military attack on January 3.

Rodriguez was previously Venezuela’s vice president. Trump has justified the attack as a law enforcement effort designed to force Maduro to “stand trial on American soil”, charging him with weapons- and drug-related crimes.

After the operation, Trump also said he planned to “run” Venezuela, and he told The Atlantic magazine that Rodriguez could “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she refuses to comply with US demands.
Since then, he has worked with the Venezuelan government to extract concessions on US priorities such as energy development and military cooperation.
Critics have accused the US of reducing Venezuela to a vassal state and exploiting its resources while leaving Maduro’s government largely intact.
Under Maduro, the Venezuelan state was accused of human rights abuses including torture, arbitrary imprisonment and extrajudicial killings.
Still, Trump has held up Venezuela as a model he would like to see replicated in other countries, like Iran and Cuba.
In Wednesday’s remarks, Hegseth said that the South American country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner”.

Rodriguez hailed the agreement as a “resumption of the technical-military relationship between both countries”, and she expressed hope that their cooperation could be “brought to its highest possible level”.
Hegseth is also set to meet with officials in Colombia later on Wednesday as part of a trip to the region.
Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora said on Tuesday that the US would deliver a C-130 Hercules military aircraft, as the US steps up military involvement across Latin America.
Hegseth has faced pressure to step down from his role, following a midterm election in which the US-Israel war on Iran contributed to Republican losses across the country.
A key member of Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth has championed the war, as well as efforts to weaken rules of engagement designed to limit civilian casualties.

Hegseth narrowly avoided a recent impeachment effort in the US Congress this month. The sponsor of that effort, outgoing Republican US Representative Thomas Massie, cited the Iran war as well as a campaign of military strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels off the coast of Latin America.
The boat-strike campaign has killed an estimated 244 people and has been denounced as extrajudicial killings by legal experts.

items.titel: $350 billion reconciliation bill ‘not going to happen’: HASC chair
items.anriss: “If a reconciliation bill is still possible, it’s going to have to be skinnied down to deal with … the hole in the defense budget that Venezuela and Iran have created,” said Rep. Mike Rogers.

absaetze.t: WASHINGTON — While a $350 billion reconciliation bill is “not going to happen,” a “skinnied down” version of the bill may still be possible, according to Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Ala., causing defense appropriators to rework the base fiscal 2027 defense spending bill to include chief priorities.

“What it looks like [is] we’re going to be able to get a reconciliation bill of some size, and by the way, $350 [billion] is not going to happen — you may have guessed that — but a reconciliation bill is still possible,” the outgoing House Armed Services Committee Chairman chairman quipped during a Hudson Institute event today.
Rogers is is not seeking a waiver to remain the top Republican on the HASC. Instead, two top competitors are lobbying for the job — Rep. Trent Kelly of Mississippi and Rep. Ronny Jackson of Texas.

His comments come as Republican lawmakers grapple with two looming deadlines. The continuing resolution that is currently funding the Pentagon is set to run out on Dec. 11, and Democrats are poised to take over both chambers on Jan. 3.

So with weeks left in control, the GOP-controlled chambers are weighing their options for a $1.5 trillion FY27 Defense Department request comprising $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in a reconciliation bill. They are also sitting on a $87.6 billion supplemental request that includes $67.1 billion in defense funds to cover expenses associated with the war in Iran.
Those three moving pieces could combine in various ways over the coming weeks.
Since the reconciliation ask included big-ticket items like Golden Dome and multi-year munition buys, Rogers said appropriators are now working on “alternatives” to funnel them into the base budget.

Senate appropriators offered up one such version this week with a plan centered on a $1.1 trillion spending bill. This summer, the House Appropriations Committee released its $1 trillion defense spending bill for fiscal 2027. Neither have been approved by the full chamber and could significantly change.
What remains unclear, Rogers said, is lawmakers’ appetite for a smaller reconciliation bill that could include defense dollars along with other “little cats and dogs.”

“If a reconciliation bill is still possible, It’s going to have to be skinnied down to deal with … the hole in the defense budget that Venezuela and Iran have created, there’s going to have to be some money for munitions stockpiles, and now we would have this FAA issue … and there’s an [agriculture] issue,” Rogers told the audience.
“But if they can skinny that reconciliation down from $350 [billion] down to $100 [billion] or somewhere in that nature, there is a path for that,” he added.

Rogers comments came as members of the Senate were having a closed-door briefing with Deputy Defense Secretary Steven Feinberg about the need for reconciliation to happen. After the briefing, Republicans after the briefing to indicated to Punchbowl News that a decision on whether to make a serious push for the defense spending could come shortly.

While Rogers’ committee oversees the annual defense policy bill that traditionally guides spending, the reconciliation request passes through the authorizers sitting on the House and Senate Armed Services Committees.

As Republicans use their final weeks to work through the spending bills, they have not yet passed the FY27 National Defense Authorization Act that contains defense policy changes ranging from troop pay raises to defense acquisition reform.

If they can get it out the door and to President Donald Trump’s desk by Jan. 3, Rogers predicted that it would not include a greenlight for the Pentagon to move out on a new Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM) proposed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“Autonomy is going to be here to stay, but it’s too premature to say that we need a command for that,” Rogers said. “But we’re having a debate. Big things don’t happen fast. … That may happen one day, but it’s just not going to happen in this year’s NDAA”
“I could be wrong,” he added. “ I mean, I’m one vote, but I have not seen it mature enough to to think that it’s going to happen this year.”
If Rogers’ prediction comes to fruition, Hegseth’s plans to stand up a new command could be on ice depending on Democrats’ priorities.

Rogers also poured cold water on any possible “right to repair” legislation this year. The initiative is aimed at giving troops the ability to fix their equipment while deployed, but industry groups have said the measure could have grave implications for intellectual property.
He said the Pentagon was unable to provide a single example of when it had been unable to not get what it wants from companies via contracts.
“If it was this big a problem, you think we’d have a list of examples, but they haven’t,” he said. “The fact is, this is something that can be contractually dealt with. They just don’t want to.
“I don’t see us changing our policy anytime in the near future,” Rogers added.

items.titel: Europe Is Exploring Orbital Deep Strike Weapons
items.anriss: Europe is beginning to explore the possibility of delivering conventional military payloads from orbit , with the German arm of defense behemoth MBDA and space transportation company ATMOS Space Cargo teaming up to investigate a concept …

absaetze.t: Europe is beginning to explore the possibility of delivering conventional military payloads from orbit, with the German arm of defense behemoth MBDA and space transportation company ATMOS Space Cargo teaming up to investigate a concept known as Precision Orbital Deep Strike (PODS). The proposal involves putting military payloads into space before sending them back through the atmosphere when commanded, potentially offering a radically different approach to long-range precision strike.

The companies announced their cooperation agreement on November 18, establishing a framework for joint feasibility studies and the design, development, and demonstration of the proposed capability. Initial work will examine system architecture, technical feasibility, payload integration, and potential technology demonstrations.

The concept is undoubtedly hugely ambitious. Getting a payload into orbit and returning it to Earth is a very different problem from developing a reliable weapon capable of striking a designated target with precision and at a predictable time. With that in mind, the agreement represents an initial effort to determine whether such a capability is technically and operationally feasible.
A New Approach To An Old Concept

The idea of using orbital trajectories to deliver weapons against targets on Earth is not new. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union developed and briefly operated a Fractional Orbital Bombardment System (FOBS), designed to place nuclear warheads into partial orbital trajectories before bringing them back toward their targets; China has more recently revisited the idea. Earlier American proposals for orbital kinetic bombardment weapons, often referred to as “Rods from God,” meanwhile explored the possibility of delivering conventional effects from space.

PODS appears to be pursuing a different approach, drawing on modern commercial orbital transportation and atmospheric re-entry technologies to potentially deliver conventional military payloads. Those payloads could consist of kinetic projectiles that simply fall from space, or perhaps some other type of munitions that emerge from a capsule after entering the atmosphere.

The London Times reported earlier this month that ATMOS had already been working on a prototype concept involving a conventional projectile carried by a satellite and protected by a re-entry vehicle. The company had reportedly been exploring military applications since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and was looking for a major defense-industry partner to help advance the concept. Now, MBDA has been identified as a potential candidate.

According to the German business newspaper Handelsblatt, the concept could eventually involve dozens of capsules operating in low Earth orbit, with military payloads held in space until needed. Low Earth Orbit (LEO) refers to a band of space that measures roughly 100 miles to 1,200 miles above the Earth, and which is highly congested. It is unclear if the plan is to use a recoverable capsule that carries a weapon, releases it during re-entry or before reaching the target, then continues to a separate recovery area, or if this is a one-way payload delivery, with the capsule and its payload expended in the strike. We have approached ATMOS for more details.
Meanwhile, ATMOS CEO Sebastian Klaus reportedly described a system intended to reach targets anywhere on Earth in less than 60 minutes.

Satellites in low Earth orbit travel at approximately 17,500 miles per hour, but this does not mean they can strike any location on Earth within a predictable timeframe. Response times will be affected by orbital inclination, spacecraft positioning, the availability of suitably positioned vehicles, re-entry requirements, and more. Achieving genuinely responsive global coverage could therefore require a substantial constellation and considerable investment in launch and replenishment infrastructure.
Commercial Space Tech Meets Military Need

ATMOS is developing reusable systems for transporting cargo into orbit and returning it to Earth. Its Phoenix program is intended to support applications including scientific research and industrial manufacturing, with atmospheric re-entry technology at the heart of the company’s approach.

These technologies could provide a starting point for the military applications now being explored with MBDA. However, the companies describe PODS as a dedicated defense initiative, separate from the civilian Phoenix program, billed as a reusable orbital transfer and return vehicle (OTRV) for autonomous cargo operations.

To date, ATMOS has demonstrated that its re-entry technology can survive an orbital flight and atmospheric entry, using its Inflatable Atmospheric Decelerator (IAD), but has not demonstrated a recoverable, independently manoeuvring orbital vehicle.

There is also a huge gulf between developing a spacecraft capable of returning cargo from orbit and creating a military delivery system capable of placing a payload accurately at a designated location. Re-entry vehicles must contend with extreme heating, rapidly changing aerodynamic conditions, and enormous stresses. Maintaining predictable flight characteristics throughout that process is already a considerable engineering challenge.

Adding a military payload introduces further complications. The system would need to account for the payload’s specific characteristics, its survivability during re-entry, and the requirements of its intended mission. Neither company has explained what kinds of military payloads are being considered or how the proposed system would achieve its intended accuracy.
It is also unclear whether PODS would involve a dedicated orbital weapons platform, individual re-entry vehicles carried into orbit, or another configuration altogether.

The hope is clearly that the combination of MBDA’s experience in missile development, guidance systems, and military payload integration, combined with ATMOS’s expertise in orbital transportation and re-entry systems, will be a meaningful starting point.
The Economics And Military Utility Remain Unclear
Even if the engineering challenges can be addressed, whether PODS would make military sense remains an open question.

A system intended to provide rapid global strike coverage from orbit could require access to launch vehicles, replacement capacity, and ground infrastructure. Maintaining such a constellation could prove expensive in comparison to the volume of kinetic strike capability they provide. In terms of numbers, German media reports suggest that “dozens” of capsules could do the job. This would be sufficient for its primary mission of striking only extremely high value and/or time sensitive targets and acting as a ‘silver bullet’ weapon system.

There would also be questions about survivability. Satellites in low Earth orbit are relatively easy to track, and their predictable orbital paths could make military platforms vulnerable to the kinds of counterspace capabilities that China and Russia are both actively engaged in. A system designed to provide persistent orbital strike options could therefore become a very attractive target in a major conflict.

The strategic advantages are clear. As well as reach, PODS would offer extreme unpredictability, a very fast response time and unconventional approach trajectories, as well as blistering speed, making it very hard to defend against. This could be enough to justify the additional expense and complexity. Having the weapon in orbit would provide better survivability than on the ground, at least in most cases.
On the other hand, space-based platforms are not inherently invulnerable, and orbital mechanics impose constraints, too.

The concept would also raise significant legal and strategic questions. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but does not contain an equivalent blanket prohibition on conventional weapons in Earth orbit. Despite that, international law governing the use of force and the conduct of hostilities would remain applicable.

There could also be consequences for strategic stability. Other countries might have difficulty distinguishing between commercial orbital transportation systems and military platforms, particularly if the latter were designed to carry payloads that could be returned to Earth at short notice. Even a conventional weapons system could be perceived as a significant strategic threat, potentially encouraging further counterspace developments.

Having said that, weaponization of space is now becoming much more common, with the ethical barrier to entry accordingly eroded. As well as Chinese and Russian activities, the United States has admitted to having orbital weapons now and the future Golden Dome will include space-based interceptors.
A European Strategic Ambition With A Long Way To Go

The statements accompanying the announcement make clear that the initiative is also intended to support Europe’s ambition to develop sovereign military capabilities. This includes efforts to establish more conventional European long-range strike capabilities, such as subsonic cruise missiles, but also emerging hyperconic capabilities.

“Europe must be able to develop, build, and operate its critical defense capabilities through its own industry — and that starts with infrastructure,” ATMOS CEO Sebastian Klaus said. He described orbital transportation and atmospheric re-entry as a new layer of strategic infrastructure, arguing that control over these technologies will determine what Europe can achieve independently.

MBDA Deutschland Managing Director Thomas Gottschild similarly described the cooperation as part of the company’s wider strategic vision in the space sector, with the aim of providing European armed forces with a sovereign capability.
Those ambitions reflect growing European interest in space as an operational domain and in reducing dependence on external suppliers for critical defense technologies, wherever they might be based.

At the same time, neither company has disclosed a development budget or an operational timetable. MBDA says that specific development activities and subsequent projects will require further evaluation and separate agreements.

The partnership is nevertheless noteworthy. It formalizes cooperation between a European space transportation company that has been exploring military applications for several years and one of the continent’s leading missile manufacturers.

Whether that combination can ultimately produce a practical orbital strike capability remains a very open question. The technical hurdles, potential costs, and uncertain military advantages are substantial. A European system fielding weapons capable of routinely striking targets from orbit remains far away in the future, if it’s even feasible. However, Europe is at least starting to explore the boundaries between commercial space transportation and conventional military strike.

absaetze.t: The latest from the fall auctions, museum protests, and tackling the British Empire one video at a time.
November 18, 2026 — 5 min read

My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.

Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work, alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution.

Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.
Really glad they worked that out.

On the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the Museum of Modern Art during an annual benefit for the museum’s Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center last Thursday, calling on filmmaker and honored guest Steven Spielberg to reject the recognition and boycott the museum over Leon Black’s Epstein-related sexual abuse allegations. Cold, biting rain soaked the group of 20 artists and activists outside the gala, and Spielberg hasn’t acknowledged their demands.

All things considered, Iraqi-British data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi’s first-ever book, which was released last week, comes at a most opportune time. The book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026), comes from Chalabi five-year endeavor in examining class inequality in the United States by analyzing the incomes, expenses, tax deductions, systemic barriers, and livelihoods of 10 Americans across the nation. In a recent interview with Hyperallergic’s Lakshmi Rivera Amin, Chalabi noted that journalists themselves often don’t acknowledge or even recognize how their own class upbringing can color their reporting on wealth and poverty, whereas other markers like race and gender are positioned as lenses of understanding.

A new video exhibition on the High Line also tackles greed and indulgence through the lens of the British Empire’s storied trade monopolies and resource theft across South Asia and China. Works by Shahzia Sikander and the artist duo Hylozoic/Desires unpack the British stronghold on salt in India and the empire’s deliberate opium influx in China during the Qing dynasty, while also highlighting historic and speculative subversions that disrupt dominant colonial narratives.

I wasn’t super fond of the High Line’s most recent film installation, but this one sounds more up my alley on a subjective, personal history level. I’m looking forward to checking it out soon — before the weather really turns south — and visiting the Mighty Miniatures exhibition that’s opening this Saturday at the National Museum of the American Indian.

November 18, 2026 — 2 min read
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.
Arpita Singh (1937–2026)Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year.

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."

items.titel: Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model
items.anriss: The group Artists 4 Artists Miami is encouraging local artists and arts workers to abstain from the city’s busy week of fairs and think more critically about ways to support the local community year-round

absaetze.t: As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Oorganisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

The campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

And yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”

According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.
“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”

items.titel: Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio among nine new products on Dezeen Showroom

absaetze.t: A table lamp comprising a plastic base topped with five magnetically attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.
Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio
Magnetic connector points are placed inside the five globe-like bulbs that light this table lamp by Hong Kong-based Canalside Studio.
The Bubbly lamp comprises a statuesque base with five bulbs attached, which can be removed and positioned around a room – including attached to metal surfaces – to spread out its ambient glow.
Other products published last week include a tile collection by Ceramiche Keope, acoustic pods by Actiu and an outdoor rug range by Rima Dain.
Read on to find out about some of our latest products:
Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope
Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope are intended to mimic the striated appearance of natural Villeneuve quartzite quarried in Italy.
As well as being striped with differently coloured striations, the tiles feature the stone’s abundance of mineral inclusions and the glinting mica microcrystals that it is studded with.
Blueroots marble by Antolini
Amber and white veining streaks across the surface of Italian stone company Antolini‘s aptly-named Blueroots marble.
The slabs can be used in kitchens and bathrooms as interior cladding or to create furnishings, imbuing interiors with visually stimulating surfaces.
Qyos acoustic pods by Actiu
Office furniture brand Actiu has evolved its Qyos acoustic pods, expanding on its configuration options and capacity for personalisation.
Described by the brand as “adaptable microarchitecture”, new options include those that enhance both aesthetics and sound absorption.
Palladia tiles by Ceramiche Refin
Italian company Ceramiche Refin‘s latest surface draws on the faceted appearance of traditional terrazzo.
Palladia comes in a trio of colourways – Iride, Luce and Aurea – and a choice of two finishes, glossy Lucida or plain Matt.
New Jetson acoustic pods by Mute
Office brand Mute‘s Jetson acoustic pods have evolved to encompass a wider range of colourways, wall layouts and levels of transparency.

Also enhanced is the pods’ acoustic credentials, which the brand says now meets Class A acoustic standards in accordance with ISO 23351-1, allowing individuals and small groups to work and converse in a quiet environment.
Outdoor rugs by Rima Dain
A range of styles, shapes and sizes are available in the catalogue of Spanish brand Rima Dain, which specialises in outdoor rugs.
Rather than being an afterthought, the rugs aim to help zone and enhance outdoor spaces in both residential and hospitality contexts.
Steel Seal washing machines by Asko
Enhanced and cutting-edge new features aim to make Swedish brand Asko‘s Steel Seal washing machines more seamless, hygienic and pleasant to use.

Two new signature technologies in particular feature in the new machines. Steel Seal, which substitutes rubber components for ones made of steel, and Quattro Construction 2.0, an integrated suspension system that reduces movement and resulting noise when in use.
One Lounge pod layout by Framery
Finnish company Framery has released an internal layout option for its One Pod, featuring a corner sofa in miniature.
One Lounge aims to make users feel at home with the cosy, thickly-padded corner seat, in place of a harder stool.
